individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces SURGE, an optimization framework that uses resurgence theory to extract critical values of the objective function from the Borel transform of a statistical-mechanical partition function Z(g)=∫ exp(-L(θ)/g)dθ. It claims singularities on the positive real axis correspond one-to-one to critical objective values, and uses these as targets to modulate the learning rate of an existing optimizer. The paper presents mathematical background on resurgence, a theoretical correspondence theorem, an analytic quartic oscillator example, and experiments on function regression, MNIST, and Shakespeare text.
Strengths: The idea of connecting Borel resummation/resurgence to non-convex optimization is original and intellectually stimulating.
The pedagogical derivation of resurgence using I(g)=∫ e^{-x}/(1-gx)dx is clear and helps motivate the framework.
The proposed wrapper approach is optimizer-agnostic and simple: scale the learning rate based on known target objective values.
The analytic quartic oscillator example shows effort to work through a nontrivial resurgent trans-series.
Weaknesses: The central theorem (Proposition/Theorem 3) is not rigorously proven and is contradicted by the paper's own quartic example: the only real critical value of V(x)=x^2+x^4 is 0, yet the computed Borel singularities are positive nonzero values (≈1.058, 2.335, ...), so they do not correspond one-to-one to critical objective values.

Equation (24) is dimensionally inconsistent: the Borel transform B[Z](t) should depend only on t, but the right-hand side contains |∇L(x)| and the level-set constraint without proper Jacobian factors; the co-area derivation in Appendix C does not yield the claimed equality and does not establish the nature of the singularities.

The asymptotic analysis of Z(g) is not justified for generic neural-network losses; no conditions are given under which Z(g) has a factorially divergent expansion, and the claim that all critical points appear as Borel singularities is unsupported.

The numerical implementation is not reproducible: algorithms appear only as redacted figure captions, result figures are redacted, and no numerical tables, baselines, or ablations are provided for the claimed 15-30% improvements.

The partition-function estimation via the variational lower bound in equation (27) lacks details on the proposal distribution qψ, optimization of c, number of samples, or accuracy; for high dimensions and small g, the method is likely impractical.
The polynomial fit of an asymptotic series from Z(g) values and the ratio-test singularity detection are heuristic and numerically unstable; no error or sensitivity analysis is provided.
The learning-rate scaling rule has no convergence guarantees and can be harmful; the authors admit instability and accelerated overfitting, so the method is not a principled extension.
The manuscript has severe presentation issues: duplicate definitions, malformed LaTeX, equation numbering errors, and undefined references, making it difficult to verify the claims.
Questions: In the quartic oscillator example, the objective's only real critical value is 0, but the Borel singularities are at ζ_k≈1.058, 2.335, ...; how is the claimed one-to-one correspondence with critical objective values consistent with this?

What are the conditions on L(θ) and the integration domain needed for Z(g) to admit a factorially divergent asymptotic series whose Borel transform has singularities exactly at the critical values of L?
How are the coupling values g_s chosen in practice, and how many series coefficients J are available/fitted? How sensitive are the detected singularities to these choices?
For the variational partition-function estimator, what proposal qψ was used in the MNIST/Shakespeare experiments, and what is the computational cost compared with the baseline optimizer?
Can you provide the actual learning-rate scaling coefficients λ and η for each experiment, and how was the target set T cleaned when spurious singularities appear?
Does the method have any theoretical convergence guarantee, even for convex losses or simple non-convex landscapes?
Limitations: The central correspondence is not valid in general; the quartic example shows singularities can occur at values that are not critical values of the objective.
The method requires estimating high-dimensional Laplace-type integrals at small g, which is computationally prohibitive without efficient samplers.
The learning-rate adaptation is ad hoc and can cause instability and overfitting; no safeguards are provided.
Experiments are not reproducible because figures are redacted and hyperparameters are missing.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper introduces SURGE (Singularity Unified Resurgent Gradient Enhancement), an optimization framework that uses resurgence theory to extract critical objective function values from the Borel transform of a partition function Z(g)=∫e^{-L(θ)/g}dθ. The authors claim that singularities of the Borel transform correspond one-to-one with critical values of the loss, and they propose an algorithm that identifies these targets and uses them to adapt the learning rate of any gradient-based optimizer. The paper presents a theoretical proposition, a two-phase algorithm, and experiments on synthetic and real datasets (though the experimental figures are redacted).
Strengths: The central idea of using resurgent asymptotics of a statistical-mechanical partition function to obtain global landscape information is original and intellectually appealing.
The method is optimizer-agnostic and proposes a concrete wrapper that could, in principle, provide global guidance to local optimizers.
The paper includes a worked quartic oscillator example in the appendix that illustrates some elements of the resurgence formalism.
Weaknesses: The main theorem is not rigorously proven: the co-area formula derivation in Appendix C contains dimensional inconsistencies and does not establish that Borel singularities correspond exactly to critical values for the real-valued partition function; it only heuristically identifies points where ∇L=0.

The asymptotic expansion of Z(g) is generally not a power series ∑ a_n g^n when the minimum of L is nonzero; the leading behavior is e^{-L*/g} times a series, which undermines the claimed Borel-transform target extraction.

The target-extraction algorithm fits a finite polynomial to Z(g) and then takes a Borel transform; the Borel transform of a polynomial is entire and has no finite singularities, so the proposed singularity-detection method (ratio test or threshold on partial sums) cannot work without additional analytic continuation or Padé approximation, which is not described in the main algorithm.

The experimental validation is incomplete: figures are redacted, no quantitative results or error bars are provided, and the abstract's claim of 15-30% improvement is not supported by any data in the manuscript.
The learning-rate adaptation rule is heuristic and not justified by the theory; no convergence guarantees are given, and the authors note that it can cause instability and accelerated overfitting.
The paper has numerous presentation issues, duplicated definitions, inconsistent notation, and malformed citations.
Questions: How does the proposed algorithm avoid the fact that the Borel transform of a finite-degree polynomial fit has no singularities?
For a loss with nonzero global minimum, what is the correct asymptotic form of Z(g), and how are Borel singularities extracted from it?
What are the exact conditions on L under which Theorem 3 holds? Does it require analyticity, compactness, or bounds on critical points?
What quantitative results were obtained in the MNIST and Shakespeare experiments? What are the hyperparameters, number of trials, and standard deviations?
How is the variational partition function estimator in Eq. (28) optimized in high dimensions, and how accurate is it when the sampler qψ is far from the target?
Why should scaling the learning rate by distance to the next lower target improve convergence? Can you provide a convergence analysis or counterexample?
Limitations: The theoretical connection is only heuristic and not validated for generic neural network losses.
The algorithm as described is not reproducible because of missing experimental details and redacted figures.
The computational cost of estimating the partition function and performing the Borel analysis scales poorly in high dimensions; no complexity analysis is given.
No discussion of failures when the loss landscape has no real critical values below the current loss or when Borel singularities lie off the real axis.
Potential negative societal impact is not discussed, though the method is general-purpose optimization and unlikely to have direct ethical concerns.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes SURGE, an optimization framework based on resurgence theory. It defines a statistical-mechanical partition function Z(g)=∫exp(-L(θ)/g)dθ for the objective L, claims that its asymptotic series coefficients grow factorially, and proposes that singularities of the Borel transform of Z(g) correspond one-to-one with objective values at critical points. These target values are then used to modulate the learning rate of any gradient-based optimizer in a wrapper. The paper includes a mathematical introduction to resurgence, a coarea-formula proof sketch, an analytic quartic-oscillator example, and descriptions of experiments on 1D regression, MNIST, and a small transformer, claiming 15-30% improvements in final objective value.
Strengths: The central idea of connecting Borel singularities of a partition function to critical values of a loss landscape is original and potentially interesting.

The quartic oscillator example in Appendix D is a concrete, worked-out illustration of trans-series and Borel-Padé resummation, showing that the authors can compute exact Borel singularities in a simple integral setting.
The proposed wrapper formulation is optimizer-agnostic and includes a graceful-degradation property when Borel analysis fails, which is practical in principle.
Weaknesses: The asymptotic expansion premise is flawed for the general case: if min L ≠ 0, Z(g) has a leading e^{-L*/g} factor and is not of the form Σ a_n g^n; the paper never explains how this exponential factor is removed before fitting power-series coefficients.

Theorem 3's claimed equality B[Z](t)=∫_{t=L(x)} dσ/|∇L| is dimensionally inconsistent as stated, and the appendix derivation does not rigorously prove a one-to-one correspondence; the singularities appear to be branch/level-set effects rather than simple poles.

The main experimental claims are unsupported: the figures are placeholders/redacted, there are no tables, error bars, hyperparameters, wall-clock comparisons, or details for the MNIST/transformer experiments, so the 15-30% improvement claim cannot be verified.

The numerical pipeline is not justified: estimating log Z variationally in high dimensions, fitting a low-order polynomial to the g-samples, and then detecting Borel singularities from noisy coefficients is highly unstable, and no guidance is given on the polynomial order J, the coupling range, or sample sizes.

The writing quality is poor: definitions are duplicated, citations contain typos, several terms (alien derivatives, Stokes constant, Lefschetz thimbles) are referenced but not adequately defined, and the key algorithms are only in appendices without sufficient reproducibility details.
Questions: For a general objective with L(θ*) = L* > 0, Z(g) behaves as exp(-L*/g) g^{d/2}(1+O(g)); how do the authors reconcile this with the assumed power-series expansion Z(g)=Σ a_n g^n?

What is the precise singularity type guaranteed by Proposition 2? The quartic example gives branch-point behavior (t-ζ)^{1/2}, not a pole; does the algorithm reliably detect such branch points with ratio tests?

How many terms J and coupling samples S are needed for accurate singularity detection in high-dimensional problems, and how sensitive are the targets to the variational sampler qψ's approximation error?
Can the authors provide actual numerical results for the MNIST and transformer experiments, including final loss values, standard deviations, and runtime overhead?
Does the SURGE learning-rate modulation have any convergence guarantee, and what happens if the closest target ζ_t is not actually reachable from the current basin?
Limitations: The paper does not provide a computational complexity analysis for the analysis phase; the variational partition-function estimator and Borel fitting may be as expensive as the optimization itself.
The method assumes critical values lie on the positive real axis and below L0, ignoring local maxima and saddles with larger values, as well as complex or negative Borel singularities.
The proof of the critical-point correspondence only sketches the coarea formula and does not handle non-isolated critical sets, flat directions, or boundary contributions.
No negative societal impact discussion is included; while none is evident, the unsupported efficiency claims could mislead practitioners into adopting an unvalidated method.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper proposes SURGE, a framework that uses resurgence theory and the Borel transform of a partition function Z(g)=∫ exp(−L(θ)/g)dθ to estimate critical values of a non-convex loss L. The claimed result is that singularities of the Borel transform correspond one-to-one with critical objective values; these values are then used to scale the learning rate of any base optimizer. The paper derives mathematical background, presents a two-phase algorithm, and reports experiments on a 1D regression, MNIST, and a small transformer.
Strengths: The high-level idea of using Borel-plane singularities of a statistical-mechanical partition function to obtain global loss-landscape information is creative and potentially inspiring.
The paper gives a self-contained introduction to resurgence and Borel summation, which may be useful to readers unfamiliar with the area.
SURGE is optimizer-agnostic and the proposed learning-rate scaling wrapper is simple to implement on top of existing optimizers.
The authors acknowledge practical issues such as instability and accelerated overfitting, showing some awareness of limitations.
Weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not rigorously established: Theorem 3's coarea-formula derivation is algebraically inconsistent (the claimed Borel transform includes a factor g and does not match the Laplace-transform representation), and Proposition 2 is contradicted by the paper's own quartic-oscillator example, where the only real critical value is 0 but the predicted Borel singularities are ≈1.0578, 2.1156, ...

The partition function Z(g) is typically ill-defined for neural-network losses because parameter space is noncompact and L does not grow in all directions; no growth/regularity assumptions are stated or verified.

The numerical estimator for Z(g) is flawed: Eq. (26) uses exp(−L/g + log q)dq, which is not an importance-sampling estimator of Z(g), and the Monte Carlo formula (25) omits the importance-weight Gaussian factor; hence the estimated c*(g) is not necessarily log Z(g).

Extracting an asymptotic series from finite noisy Z(g) values and locating Borel singularities by ratio tests/direct evaluation is numerically ill-conditioned and unsupported; no Padé methods, error bounds, or conditioning analysis are provided.

The experiments are presented only through redacted figures and qualitative bullet points; there are no numerical results, hyperparameters, runs, or error bars to support the claimed 15–30% improvements, making the validation unverifiable.

The manuscript has serious presentation defects: duplicated definitions, broken cross-references, malformed equations, inconsistent notation, and a mathematically incorrect hypergeometric expression in Appendix D.
Questions: How is Z(g) guaranteed to converge for the neural-network losses considered, given symmetries and noncompact parameter directions?
Can you provide a step-by-step derivation of B[Z](t)=∫_{t=L(x)} dσ(x)/|∇L(x)| that removes the spurious factor g and reconciles the dimensions with the definition of the Borel transform?

In the quartic example V=x^2+x^4, the only real critical value is 0, but the computed Borel singularities are ≈1.0578 and 2.1156; what are the corresponding critical points, and why do they not appear in Proposition 2?
Please write the exact importance-sampling estimator for Z(g), including the proposal density, and explain how Eq. (28) maximizes log Z.
How many coupling points g and series orders J were used for MNIST/transformer? How did you verify the fitted series is asymptotic and that the detected singularities are stable?
What happens when no Borel singularity lies below the current loss value? Does SURGE then become a standard optimizer?
What are the exact final loss values and training epochs for each optimizer in the reported figures, with standard errors?
Limitations: The theoretical analysis assumes the loss has isolated, nondegenerate real critical points and that the partition-function integral converges; these assumptions are not verified for modern neural nets.
Partition-function estimation in high dimensions is a hard sampling problem; the proposed variational estimator is not shown to scale or be accurate.
The use of Borel targets is only a crude learning-rate multiplier; it can cause instability and overfitting, as the authors note, and it may guide the optimizer toward spurious targets.
Positive-real singularities below L0 may be absent even when meaningful lower critical values exist, limiting applicability.
No experiments on large-scale models or standard benchmarks with complete quantitative results are presented.

review.Summary: The paper proposes SURGE, an optimization framework that uses resurgence theory and Borel transform singularities of a statistical-mechanical partition function Z(g)=∫e^{-L(θ)/g}dθ to extract critical objective-function values as global guidance. After a one-time analysis phase that estimates Z(g) at small couplings and locates Borel-plane singularities, the method wraps any gradient optimizer and scales the learning rate depending on proximity to these target values. The authors claim a rigorous correspondence between Borel singularities and critical objective values, and report improved convergence on synthetic and real benchmarks, though experimental figures are redacted.
Strengths: The paper introduces a novel cross-disciplinary idea: using resurgence theory and Borel transforms to extract global landscape information for optimization, which is conceptually interesting and differs from typical heuristics.
Section 2.1 provides an accessible, tutorial-style introduction to Borel summation and resurgence, including the instructive divergent-series example.
The SURGE wrapper is optimizer-agnostic and conceptually simple, potentially allowing integration with existing optimizers.

The quartic-oscillator appendix demonstrates a worked analytic example of Borel-Padé resummation and trans-series reconstruction, illustrating the mechanics of resurgence in a one-dimensional setting.
Weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is contradicted by the paper's own Appendix D example: for V(x)=x²+x⁴, the Borel singularities are stated to be ζ_k=(2^{5/3}/3)k≈1.0578k, while the critical values of V are 0 (at x=0) and -1/4 (at complex critical points). These do not match, so the claimed one-to-one correspondence between Borel singularities and critical objective values is unsupported and false at least in this case.

The proof of Theorem 3 is mathematically invalid. The co-area-formula manipulation leads to an expression for the Borel transform that spuriously contains a factor of g (or is inconsistent between the main text and appendix), and the resulting equality cannot imply that singularities occur exactly at critical values of L.

The assumed asymptotic expansion Z(g)∼∑a_n g^n is unjustified. In the quartic-oscillator example, the leading behavior is √(π g) times a power series, so the expansion contains fractional powers of g; the Borel coefficients are not well-defined as stated for general L.

The experimental validation is essentially absent: all figures comparing SURGE with base optimizers are redacted, no numerical results, hyperparameters, number of runs, or standard deviations are provided, and the claimed 15–30% improvements are unsubstantiated.

The computational feasibility of estimating Z(g) for small g in high-dimensional neural-network parameter spaces is not established. The variational estimator of log Z requires solving a difficult optimization problem for each g, and as g→0 the integrand becomes exponentially concentrated, likely making variance or bias unmanageable; no complexity or error analysis is given.

The learning-rate adjustment heuristic is ad hoc: selecting ζ_t and multiplying η by α has no theoretical justification, no convergence guarantee, and the authors admit it creates instability and can accelerate overfitting, undermining the claim of principled global guidance.

The manuscript has many presentation issues, including duplicated definitions, inconsistent notation, a sign error in the residue computation (1+ζ vs 1−ζ), unresolved [REDACTED] placeholders, and malformed equations, which make it difficult to assess reproducibility.
Questions: For the quartic oscillator V(x)=x²+x⁴, the Borel singularities are at ζ_k≈1.0578k, but the critical values of V are 0 and -0.25. How does this example support the claimed one-to-one correspondence between Borel singularities and critical objective values?
What is the precise asymptotic expansion of Z(g)=∫e^{-L(θ)/g}dθ for a generic smooth L? If it includes fractional powers such as g^{d/2}, how are the Borel coefficients a_n defined and extracted?

Can the proof of Theorem 3 be made rigorous? In particular, what is the correct co-area-formula identity relating the Borel transform to level-set integrals, and why should its singularities occur exactly at critical values rather than at differences of critical actions?

How is the variational estimator of log Z(g) biased or bounded when g is very small and the Boltzmann weight e^{-L/g} is concentrated on rare low-loss regions? What is the computational cost in high dimensions?

What are the exact experimental settings for the reported MNIST and Shakespeare experiments: model architectures, data splits, hyperparameters, number of independent runs, and quantitative results? The provided figures are redacted.
How sensitive is the target set T to the truncation order J, the threshold τ, and the choice of coupling range? Are there failure cases where the Borel analysis produces no or incorrect targets?
Does the SURGE learning-rate scaling α^(k) preserve any convergence guarantees of the base optimizer? Is there a theoretical analysis of the update rule?
Limitations: The theoretical correspondence between Borel singularities and critical objective values is not established and is false for the paper's own analytic example, so the method lacks a valid mathematical foundation as presented.

Computing the partition function Z(g) for small coupling in high-dimensional parameter spaces is likely intractable or extremely expensive; the paper provides no complexity analysis or empirical cost estimates.

The method requires fitting an asymptotic series to partition-function estimates and locating Borel singularities, both of which are numerically fragile and introduce approximation error that is not quantified.
The learning-rate controller can destabilize training, as admitted, and may accelerate overfitting when the base optimizer already generalizes poorly.
No comparison is made to other global-optimization or saddle-point-escaping methods, only to standard optimizers, and even those comparisons are missing due to redacted figures.
Potential negative societal impacts are not discussed, although as a general optimization method the direct risks appear low.

review.Summary: The paper introduces SURGE, an optimization framework that uses resurgence theory and the Borel transform of a statistical-mechanical partition function Z(g)=∫exp(-L(θ)/g)dθ to extract critical objective values. The authors claim that singularities of the Borel transform correspond one-to-one to critical values of the loss, and use these targets to modulate the learning rate of any gradient-based optimizer. The paper provides mathematical background on resurgence, a theoretical proposition, a quartic oscillator example, and experiments on regression, MNIST, and a small transformer, claiming 15-30% improvements.
Strengths: The high-level idea of connecting Borel-plane singularities of a partition function to global loss-landscape information is original and intellectually stimulating.
The paper gives an accessible, tutorial-style introduction to Borel summation and resurgence, which may be useful to readers unfamiliar with the area.
The SURGE wrapper is optimizer-agnostic and conceptually simple, potentially allowing integration with existing optimizers.
The quartic-oscillator appendix demonstrates a concrete worked analysis of Borel-Padé resummation and trans-series reconstruction.
Weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not rigorously established and is contradicted by the paper's own quartic-oscillator example: the objective V(x)=x²+x⁴ has a critical value 0, yet the computed Borel singularities are ≈1.0578, 2.1156, ...; these do not match, so the asserted one-to-one correspondence is unsupported.

The asymptotic expansion of Z(g) is not justified for generic neural-network losses; if the minimum of L is nonzero, Z(g) behaves as e^{-L*/g} times a power series, and the paper does not explain how this exponential factor is handled.

The proof of Theorem 3 contains dimensional inconsistencies and relies on a co-area-formula derivation that does not establish the claimed singularity structure; it only heuristically identifies points where ∇L=0.

The numerical pipeline for extracting Borel singularities is flawed: the Borel transform of a finite-degree polynomial fit has no singularities, so the proposed ratio-test or threshold-based detection cannot work without additional analytic continuation (e.g., Padé approximation), which is not described.

The partition-function estimator is not justified: the variational importance-sampling formula appears incorrect (omitting the importance-weight factor), and high-dimensional estimation for small g is likely intractable or extremely expensive.

The experiments are incomplete and not reproducible: results figures are redacted, no quantitative values, hyperparameters, baselines, error bars, or ablations are provided, making the claimed 15-30% improvements unverifiable.

The learning-rate scaling rule is heuristic, has no convergence guarantees, and the authors admit it can cause instability and accelerated overfitting, undermining the claim of principled global guidance.

The manuscript has severe presentation issues, including duplicated definitions, malformed equations, broken cross-references, and undefined symbols, making it difficult to verify the technical claims.
Questions: For V(x)=x²+x⁴, the only real critical value is 0, but Borel singularities are at ≈1.0578 and 2.1156; how is the claimed one-to-one correspondence consistent with this?
What are the precise conditions on L(θ) under which Z(g) admits a factorially divergent power series ∑a_n g^n, and how is the e^{-L*/g} factor handled when L* > 0?
How does the algorithm detect singularities from a Borel transform of a fitted polynomial, which is entire and has no finite singularities? Is Padé approximation used?
What are the exact importance-sampling estimators for Z(g) and log Z(g)? Why does Eq. (26) omit the importance-weight Gaussian factor?
What are the full experimental details and quantitative results for the MNIST and Shakespeare experiments, including architectures, hyperparameters, number of runs, and standard deviations?
Does the SURGE learning-rate modulation preserve any convergence guarantees of the base optimizer, and what happens when no Borel singularity lies below the current loss?
Limitations: The theoretical correspondence between Borel singularities and critical objective values is not established and is false for the paper's own analytic example.
Computing Z(g) for small g in high-dimensional parameter spaces is likely intractable or extremely expensive; no complexity analysis or empirical cost estimates are provided.
The method's numerical components (fit of asymptotic series, Borel singularity detection) are fragile and lack error or sensitivity analysis.
The learning-rate controller can destabilize training and may accelerate overfitting, as admitted by the authors.
Experiments are not reproducible because figures are redacted and hyperparameters are missing, so the claimed improvements are unsubstantiated.
No comparison to other global-optimization or saddle-point-escaping methods is made.
